title: Probabilistic frontier prioritization
description: Soft cluster memberships and information gain help UAV teams prioritize viewpoints as an unknown environment is mapped.
introduction: When several UAVs explore an unknown area, rigid frontier groups can restrict useful choices and duplicate work. This method uses soft clustering to keep viewpoint priorities flexible as the map evolves.

problem.heading: A changing map needs flexible choices.
paragraphs: Frontiers mark the boundary between known free space and unexplored space. Grouping them helps a team divide its work, but hard cluster boundaries can separate nearby, useful viewpoints.
As new measurements change the map, those boundaries can constrain the next decision. The aim is to preserve useful alternatives while reducing redundant exploration.

method.heading: Soft memberships. Informative viewpoints.
paragraphs: A Dirichlet-process Gaussian mixture model represents candidate viewpoints with graded cluster memberships and adapts model complexity to the frontier distribution.
The method combines expected information gain with cluster coherence to form a probabilistic priority. A compatible exploration planner then uses that priority to choose its next motion.

This is a modular prioritization mechanism demonstrated with FAME and Frontier Shepherding (FroShe). Memberships relate viewpoints to mixture components; they are not a hard assignment of every frontier to a robot.

evidenceIntroduction: Simulation measures changes in exploration time against defined baselines. Outdoor trials demonstrate the feasibility of the two-UAV system.
simulationContext: Across tested team sizes and forest densities, with unrestricted communication. Each planner is compared with its own enhanced version.
hardwareContext: Two UAVs using the FAME-based implementation explored an outdoor court. The endpoint was 95% coverage in each trial.
hardwareNote: These three trials demonstrate hardware feasibility. They are separate from the simulated percentage improvements above.
